body_markdown:
We won’t bury the lede here: The real question is whether the Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale’s simulated manual transmission can pass as a true manual. The answer is a resounding *yes* .


With, of course, some caveats. All of which you can learn about by watching our “Jason Cammisa on the ICONS” episode on YouTube below, which includes a full test of the Manuale and a history lesson about transmissions.


Back to the car.


This is Ferrari’s first “manual-transmission” car in a decade and a half, but nothing in the powertrain is new. Under the bodywork, it’s the same as every other 12Cilindri, with the same 9500-rpm, 819-horsepower, 6.5-liter V-12 connected to an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic.


The hardware changes are limited to a physical start button rather than the regular Dodici’s capacitive embarrassment (yay!), a steering column devoid of paddles, a clutch pedal, and a gated shifter with six forward gears and reverse in a traditional H-pattern.


Ferrari/Kai Grossmann


Once again, what Ferrari has created is a new interface. (Its last new interface was the shift paddle—something that’s now become entirely conventional.) The shifter has a cam-and-spring mechanism to recreate the “feel” of a shifter, and the external gate is tuned to make the sound of Ferrari shifters of yore. It works.


A solenoid prevents the shifter from entering a gear, and the computer monitors the position of the shifter to either lock it out from engaging a gear that would overrev the engine, or to slow down the shifter to stop it from going into a gear until the transmission has actually engaged it. (It does this, cleverly, by watching the speed and trajectory of the shifter and comparing it to the actual synchro speeds in the transmission.) It’s unobtrusive and feels no different from a real manual transmission that doesn’t want to be hurried.


None of this prevents you from shifting this transmission incredibly quickly. You’ll only notice a delay if you’re trying to beat the synchros when going to a gear that’s on the same DCT shaft as the previous gear (i.e. 4th to 2nd).


## **Specs: 2026** Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale


**Base Price:** Est. $662,000
**Powertrain:** DOHC 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V-12, eight-speed dual-clutch automatic, manually shiftable through the first six gears
**Output:** 819 hp @ 9250 rpm, 500 lb-ft @ 7250 rpm
**Layout:** front-engine, rear-wheel-drive, two-door, two-seat coupe
**Weight:** 3450 pounds dry weight
**0–60 mph:** 2.9 sec
**EPA-rated Fuel Economy:** TBA
**Competitors:** Bentley Continental GT Speed


The hardest part of driving a manual, of course, is getting it off the line. And that’s what we assumed would be the hardest part to get right for a simulation. It’s not the case, however, said the system’s chief engineer; the computer is simply instructed to follow what the clutch pedal is doing.


Meaning, you can stall the Manuale if you aren’t careful. You can overrev it and buck. Other than the clutch’s engagement point taking place over a larger-than-normal amount of pedal stroke, it feels entirely natural.


What isn’t natural, however, is the throttle mapping. The V-12 has no flywheel, and it revs up and down instantly. To calm the regular 12Cilindri’s overly aggressive throttle response, the engineering team uploaded a second throttle map to tone down the response any time the clutch is depressed. It’s brilliant—better than the regular mapping, in fact—but the transition between the two of them is obvious if you’re paying attention.


Ferrari/Kai Grossmann


In normal driving, there is no way you’d know that the interface is by-wire only, rather than physical. It’s *that* convincing. And it transforms the 12Cilindri experience. Suddenly, you’re engaging directly with a naturally aspirated V-12 in a completely new way.


We drove the Manuale only at Ferrari’s Fiorano test track, which seemed to shrink by some measure; the 12Cilindri’s outrageous speed combined with the manual transmission meant constant shifting. After driving the Manuale in Ferrari’s backyard, it’s obvious why the automaker has insisted on automatic gearboxes for so long. Given the circuit’s tight confines, it’s a wonder Ferrari hasn’t been building Miatas.


Slow the pace down, however, and drive like you would on the road, and the Manuale is a revelation—much, much more interactive and enjoyable than the dual-clutch car.


Ferrari has said it benchmarked its own cars for shift feel. That’s not a particularly good thing, because the last of its manuals weren’t particularly good: The externally gated shifter was a mismatch for its partner engine’s super-light rotating assembly. Because of those cars’ light flywheels (which Ferrari undoubtedly installed to assist the F1 automated manuals’ lightning-quick shifts) the revs fell to idle almost instantly when you declutched and let off the gas. At the same time, the long shift throws meant the shift took much longer. As a result, the best way to shift was to do it as quickly as your muscles would let you, which felt mechanically unsympathetic to the extreme. Blipping the throttle while shifting, to keep the revs up, was an alternative. Though not a dealbreaker, those characteristics meant that the final Ferrari manuals weren’t as pleasurable to drive as the best contemporary manual ’boxes around.


Ferrari/Lorenzo Marcinno


Those same elements of light rotating mass (remember, the Manuale has no flywheel at all) and long throws are present in the 12Cilindri, but since you’re not actually moving through gears with the shifter, there’s no need to be concerned with preserving mechanical pieces. In other words, the shifter feels brand-appropriate for Ferrari, only better.


There is no automatic rev-matching (hallelujah!), but getting the revs right on a downshift takes some fine motor control of your right foot. And the instantaneousness of the throttle highlights a small but significant delay in the by-wire brake system—something that was never obvious in the DCT. (The two cars use the same brake system, so interestingly, this discrepancy comes down to expectations. The “manual” car feels analog, so it highlights any other “bugs” in the powertrain.)


Ferrari engineers have said (to us) for years that they not only weren’t willing to put a manual transmission in their cars, but that they *couldn’t* : The manual was too much of a blind spot in the chassis control systems that help the cars perform at the lofty levels they do. This new manual-interface-on-a-DCT solves that problem, and the chassis control systems still ultimately have final say in clutch engagement in case of emergency.


Ferrari/Kai Grossmann


Of course, the system can also re-engage full-automatic mode (more on that later) in an emergency, for example, when adaptive cruise control is activated and Automatic Emergency Braking activates. However, despite blowing through a tank of gas and a set of tires on the track, even with a spin or two while drifting for camera, never once did the system fail to follow this driver’s wishes.


We could, however, trick it. Cruising in second gear, we tripped up the system by pretending to upshift into third but then suddenly going into first. If executed quicker than the computer was able to lock out the gear in the shifter (we’d let go of the clutch, letting the engine freewheel for a half-second or so before) … *bang!* It violently engaged first.


The other glitch I noticed is that the shifter can be pushed out of gear with the engine under load—not possible in a real manual-transmission car. This can’t be fixed with software, since the solenoid can only prevent going into a gear, not coming out of one.


There are other small bugs that can be fixed with software—and probably should be. The first is that the system will not switch from automatic mode into manual mode at speeds over 70 km/h (approximately 43 mph). Ferrari says this is for safety reasons, because each mode is so distinct that switching between them requires an adjustment. They’re not strictly wrong, but since the Manuale lacks paddles, this creates a problem: In manual mode, there are only six gates to control eight gears, and Ferrari solved this by locking out the two numerically highest gears. Top gear occurs in seventh, so that’s inaccessible, but likely irrelevant, especially in the U.S.


Ferrari/Lorenzo Marcinno


On the other hand, highway cruising will be done in a maximum of sixth gear, which is, in fact, quite short. (U.S.-speed highway cruising will require nearly 4000 rpm.) To reduce revs, the driver must shift into automatic mode but is then locked there until vehicle speed falls below 43 mph.


With shift paddles, this wouldn’t be too big of a deal—except that the Manuale lacks them. And Ferrari’s head-scratching decision (for 15 years, now) to *not* offer full kickdown in automatic mode results in a markedly slower 12Cilindri during passing maneuvers.


This is a decision I firmly believe Ferrari should fix anyway. But an easier solution would be to allow the shifter to function as a Tiptronic-type shift lever when in automatic mode. When the solenoid is energized to lock out a gear, the lever is allowed to travel roughly halfway up that gate before it’s stopped, and then it is spring-loaded to return to the neutral position. So, forward-for-downshift into the third-gear gate and backward-for-upshift into the fourth-gear gate would be as easy to implement as a few lines of code.


The other potential software fix would be to instruct the transmission to engage eighth gear in the transmission when the shifter is in sixth. Or even seventh. Or, better yet, to allow the driver, in a menu, to decide which gear they prefer.


Ferrari


The mere fact that we’re discussing minutiae like this, however, highlights how incredibly good the system is, on its first outing. The most difficult stuff—making it feel like a real manual in normal driving—is what Ferrari absolutely nailed.


Maranello could have, of course, just installed a regular manual transmission in the car. But that would have taken years and millions of dollars of investment to develop and test. There exists no manual in production today that would accept this V-12’s combination of torque and revs, so one would have to be made—and validated—from scratch. And, of course, having a real manual would prevent the 12Cilindri Manuale from being able to achieve the same acceleration numbers as the DCT version. Since the Manuale can be run in Automatic DCT mode, Ferrari can claim the same 0–62 mph time as the regular car.


Of far more importance than you likely realize is the fact that Ferrari can also claim the same fuel-economy, CO2-emissions, and drive-by noise numbers as the base car. This represents an easy seven-figure-dollar cost savings because the Manuale does not need re-certification.


All of that adds up to a money savings that doesn’t extend to the customer, one can deduce. The Manuale’s MSRP is some $209,000 greater than the regular 12Cilindri (though it does include some other detail changes). Given a planned 1499-car production run, this means Ferrari is booking more than $300 million in incremental (read: additional!) revenue for this project.


Ferrari/Lorenzo Marcinno


One that certainly cost less than that to complete. Ferrari once again turns an engineering project into a cash machine. And in doing so, it has put into production a new type of transmission interface that will, if this car is any indication, almost certainly be copied by other manufacturers. (You may argue that Koenigsegg already produced a similar system, but the production volume of that system is infinitesimally small.)


First the F1 paddles, now the Manuale—Ferrari has, once again, invented a transmission interface that will one day be common. On top of that, it finally delivers on the failed promise of every DCT before it: all of the benefits of a manual with all of the benefits of an automatic. And without the drawbacks of either.


Learn more (and watch the 12Cilindri Manuale in action) on YouTube[here](https://youtu.be/-5vuipaI7l0) .


Ferrari/Lorenzo Marcinno
